ap_chemistry-f01.title: Permanganate titration of iron in an ore

stimulus.description: A student dissolves a $0.900\text{ g}$ sample of iron ore in acid so that all of the iron is present as Fe²⁺ and dilutes the solution to $100.00\text{ mL}$. A $25.00\text{ mL}$ portion is titrated with $0.0200\text{ M}$ KMnO₄. The balanced equation is MnO₄⁻ + 5 Fe²⁺ + 8 H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5 Fe³⁺ + 4 H₂O. The endpoint is reached after $26.80\text{ mL}$ of KMnO₄ has been added.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of MnO₄⁻ added at the endpoint and the number of moles of Fe²⁺ in the $25.00\text{ mL}$ portion.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the moles of MnO₄⁻ (about 5.360e-04 mol)
common_errors: uses the volume in mL without converting to liters

rubric_rows.criterion: Multiplies by 5 for the moles of Fe²⁺ (about 2.680e-03 mol)
common_errors: uses a 1:1 mole ratio

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass percent of iron in the ore sample.
parts.model_answer: The 100.00 mL solution holds 4 × 2.680e-03 = 1.072e-02 mol Fe, which is 0.5987 g; mass percent = 0.5987/0.900 × 100 = 66.5%.

rubric_rows.criterion: Scales the moles of Fe²⁺ from the 25.00 mL portion to the 100.00 mL solution (about 1.072e-02 mol)
common_errors: uses only the moles in the 25.00 mL portion

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the mass percent of iron by converting to the mass of iron and dividing by the ore mass (about 66.5%)
common_errors: divides by the mass of the portion instead of the whole sample

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: No indicator was added to the flask. Explain how the student can still identify the endpoint.
parts.model_answer: MnO₄⁻ is purple and is reduced to nearly colorless Mn²⁺ while Fe²⁺ remains; once all of the Fe²⁺ has reacted, the first excess drop of MnO₄⁻ leaves a faint persistent pink color.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the endpoint is the first persistent pink or purple color
common_errors: says the solution becomes colorless at the endpoint

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that MnO₄⁻ is consumed (reduced to colorless Mn²⁺) until the Fe²⁺ is gone, so the excess MnO₄⁻ colors the solution
common_errors: says Fe²⁺ itself produces the pink color

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A bubble was trapped in the tip of the buret before the titration and left the tip during the titration. Will the calculated mass percent of iron be too high, too low, or unaffected? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Too high: the bubble volume is counted as titrant delivered, so the recorded volume is larger than the volume that reacted.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the mass percent of iron will be too high
common_errors: says it will be too low

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the buret reading overstates the volume of KMnO₄ that reacted, which overstates the moles of Fe²⁺
common_errors: says the concentration of KMnO₄ changes

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Identify the oxidizing agent in the reaction and justify your answer using oxidation numbers.
parts.model_answer: MnO₄⁻ is the oxidizing agent: the oxidation number of Mn decreases from +7 to +2, so MnO₄⁻ is reduced and oxidizes Fe²⁺.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies MnO₄⁻ as the oxidizing agent
common_errors: identifies Fe²⁺ as the oxidizing agent

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites the change in the oxidation number of Mn from +7 to +2, showing that it is reduced
common_errors: uses the oxidation number of iron without noting that it increases

ap_chemistry-f02.title: Method of initial rates and the rate law

stimulus.description: Initial rates for A + B → products at one temperature

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Determine the order of the reaction with respect to A and with respect to B. Justify each answer with the data.
parts.model_answer: Doubling [A] with [B] fixed multiplies the rate by 2, so the order in A is 1; doubling [B] with [A] fixed multiplies the rate by 4, so the order in B is 2.

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the order 1 in A by comparing experiments 1 and 2 (rate ratio 2)
common_errors: compares experiments in which both concentrations change

rubric_rows.criterion: Finds the order 2 in B by comparing experiments 1 and 3 (rate ratio 4)
common_errors: uses the coefficient from the equation

rubric_rows.criterion: Relates each rate ratio to the factor by which the concentration changed
common_errors: gives the orders without using the data

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Write the rate law for the reaction and calculate the value of the rate constant, including units.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes rate = k[A]^1[B]^2
common_errors: includes a product or a concentration with the wrong exponent

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates k (about 0.04 M⁻² s⁻¹) with units
common_errors: omits the units of k

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the initial rate when [A]₀ = 0.05 M and [B]₀ = 0.4 M.

rubric_rows.criterion: Substitutes the concentrations into the rate law
common_errors: uses the concentrations of experiment 1

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the rate (about 3.200e-04 M/s)
common_errors: adds the terms instead of multiplying

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The temperature is increased and the experiments are repeated. The rate constant increases. Explain this increase in terms of the molecules that react.
parts.model_answer: A larger fraction of collisions has energy at least equal to the activation energy at the higher temperature, so more collisions are effective and the rate constant is larger.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that a larger fraction of collisions has enough energy to react
common_errors: says the activation energy decreases

rubric_rows.criterion: Connects the energy to the activation energy at the higher temperature
common_errors: says the concentration of the reactants increases

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: A student proposes that the reaction occurs in a single elementary step A + B → products. Is the proposal consistent with the rate law? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Not consistent: for a single elementary step the rate law would be rate = k[A][B], which does not match the experimental orders 1 and 2.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the proposal is not consistent because an elementary step has orders equal to its coefficients, rate = k[A][B]
common_errors: decides from the coefficient of the overall equation without considering the experimental orders

ap_chemistry-f03.title: Gravimetric analysis of chloride

stimulus.description: A student dissolves a $0.500\text{ g}$ sample of an unknown chloride salt in water and adds excess AgNO₃(aq). The AgCl precipitate is filtered, washed, dried, and found to have a mass of $1.100\text{ g}$. The molar mass of AgCl is 143.32 g/mol, and the molar mass of Cl is 35.45 g/mol.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the precipitation reaction.
parts.model_answer: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) with phases
common_errors: includes spectator ions in the equation

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of AgCl formed and the mass of chloride in the sample.

rubric_rows.criterion: Divides the mass of AgCl by its molar mass (about 0.00768 mol)
common_errors: multiplies by the molar mass

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the moles of Cl⁻ equal the moles of AgCl (1:1)
required_elements: moles of Cl- equal moles of AgCl
common_errors: uses the mole ratio of the salt instead of the chloride

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the mass of chloride (about 0.2721 g)
common_errors: uses the molar mass of AgCl

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass percent of chloride in the unknown salt.

rubric_rows.criterion: Divides the mass of chloride by the mass of the sample
common_errors: divides by the mass of the precipitate

rubric_rows.criterion: Expresses the result as about 54.4%
common_errors: leaves the result as a fraction

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: A student forgets to dry the precipitate completely before finding its mass. Predict the effect on the calculated mass percent of chloride, and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Too high: wet precipitate has extra mass from water, so the mass of AgCl is too large and the moles of Cl⁻ are overestimated.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the mass percent will be too high
common_errors: says the result will be too low

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that the extra water adds mass to the precipitate, overstating the moles of AgCl and Cl⁻
common_errors: says the water reacts with the chloride

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: The student repeats the experiment but uses too little AgNO₃(aq), so some chloride remains in solution. Explain why the calculated mass percent would be incorrect.
parts.model_answer: Too low: AgNO₃ would be the limiting reactant, so less AgCl forms than the chloride in the sample could produce.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the calculated mass percent would be too low
common_errors: says the result would be unaffected

rubric_rows.criterion: States that not all of the chloride precipitates, so the mass of AgCl underestimates the chloride in the sample
common_errors: says the excess AgNO₃ lowers the mass of AgCl

ap_chemistry-f05.title: Types of solids and their properties

stimulus.description: A student compares the properties of two solids, NaCl and SiO₂. NaCl is an ionic solid, and SiO₂ is a covalent network solid.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe the species that make up NaCl and the type of attraction that holds them in place.
parts.model_answer: NaCl is a ionic solid: positive and negative ions held by electrostatic attractions.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describes the species and the ionic attraction
common_errors: describes discrete molecules held by dispersion forces

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Compare the electrical conductivity of NaCl and SiO₂, and explain the difference in terms of charged species that can or cannot move.
parts.model_answer: NaCl conducts electricity when melted but not as a solid, and SiO₂ does not conduct in either state: mobile ions are present in the liquid but not in the solid; the network solid has no mobile charged particles.

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares the conductivity as: NaCl conducts electricity when melted but not as a solid, and SiO₂ does not conduct in either state
common_errors: says all solids with strong bonds conduct

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the difference using mobile or fixed charged species
common_errors: explains with molar mass

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Predict which of the two solids has the higher melting point and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: SiO₂ has the higher melting point: a covalent network must break strong covalent bonds throughout the solid.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts the higher melting point and links it to the strength of the bonding throughout the solid
common_errors: says melting breaks covalent bonds in all solids

ap_chemistry-f06.title: Intermolecular forces and boiling points of the hydrogen halides

stimulus.description: Molar masses and normal boiling points of four hydrogen halides

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe the trend in the boiling points of HCl, HBr, and HI, and explain the trend in terms of intermolecular forces.
parts.model_answer: The boiling point increases from HCl to HI; as the number of electrons increases, the electron cloud is more polarizable, so London dispersion forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the boiling point increases from HCl to HBr to HI (188 K to 206 K to 237 K)
common_errors: says the boiling point decreases as the molar mass increases

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that the larger, more polarizable electron clouds give stronger London dispersion forces
common_errors: says the covalent H–X bonds are stronger in HI

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: HF has the lowest molar mass in the table but a higher boiling point than HCl and HBr. Explain this observation.
parts.model_answer: HF molecules form hydrogen bonds (H bonded to F attracts a lone pair on another F), which are stronger than the dipole–dipole and dispersion forces in HCl and HBr.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies hydrogen bonding between HF molecules as stronger than the intermolecular forces in HCl and HBr
common_errors: says the H–F covalent bond breaks when the liquid boils

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Predict whether the vapor pressure of HF at 250 K is higher or lower than the vapor pressure of HCl at 250 K, and justify your answer using the data in the table.
parts.model_answer: Lower: HF has the higher normal boiling point, so its intermolecular forces are stronger, fewer molecules escape from the liquid at a given temperature, and the vapor pressure is lower.

rubric_rows.criterion: Predicts the lower vapor pressure for HF because its higher boiling point (293 K versus 188 K) indicates stronger intermolecular forces
common_errors: says a higher boiling point means a higher vapor pressure

ap_chemistry-f07.title: ICE table and equilibrium concentrations

stimulus.description: For the gas-phase reaction A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g), a student starts a rigid container with $0.5\text{ M}$ of A and $0.5\text{ M}$ of B and no C. At equilibrium at a fixed temperature, the concentration of C is $0.1\text{ M}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the equilibrium constant expression and calculate the equilibrium concentrations of A and B.
parts.model_answer: [A] = 0.5 − 0.1 = 0.4 M and [B] = 0.5 − 0.1 = 0.4 M, because each mole of C formed uses one mole of A and one of B.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes Kc = [C]/([A][B])
common_errors: puts the reactants in the numerator

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates [A] = 0.4 M and [B] = 0.4 M
common_errors: subtracts twice the change

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the value of Kc.

rubric_rows.criterion: Substitutes into the expression for about 0.625
common_errors: uses the initial concentrations

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the value of Kc for the reverse reaction, C(g) ⇌ A(g) + B(g), at the same temperature.
parts.model_answer: For the reverse reaction, K = 1/Kc = 1/0.625 = 1.600.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the value of the reciprocal of Kc (about 1.600)
common_errors: uses the same value of Kc for the reverse reaction
